findings.title: paginate() called with unsupported enable_advanced_features kwarg
findings.body: The optimized branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). The base endpoint's paginate() helper has an explicit parameter list (request, queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, cursor_serializer, max_limit, etc.) and does not forward arbitrary **kwargs to the paginator constructor, so this call raises a TypeError. Any superuser (or user with global access) hitting GET /api/0/organizations/<org>/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true will get a 500 instead of a paginated response. The flag also needs to be plumbed through properly or the feature removed.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator negative-offset path crashes: Django ORM does not support negative slicing
findings.body: The new 'advanced feature' branch slices the queryset with a negative start (queryset[start_offset:stop] where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), and both the code comment and the class docstring claim 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') for any negative slice bound. So whenever enable_advanced_features=True and a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, the request fails with an unhandled AssertionError instead of returning a page. The entire advertised feature is broken as written.

findings.title: BasePaginator.get_result now silently clamps negative offsets, changing behavior for all existing paginators
findings.body: The shared BasePaginator.get_result was changed from `stop = offset + limit + extra; queryset[offset:stop]` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For a forward cursor with a negative offset, the ORM previously raised (negative slicing is unsupported), which surfaced malformed/crafted cursors; now it silently rewinds to offset 0 and returns the first page while build_cursor still carries the negative offset into the next cursor (next_offset = offset + limit in _build_next_values), producing corrupt pagination state. For is_prev cursors the negative offset is still passed through and crashes. This is an unrelated behavior change to a base class used by many endpoints, made in a PR whose stated purpose is the spans buffer.

findings.title: Span-count guard removed; eviction is silent and max_segment_spans config is now dead
findings.body: This PR removes the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` check from _load_segment_data and replaces it with zpopmin eviction inside the Lua script (add-buffer.lua, `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...)`). Consequences: (1) spans are now silently dropped from segments at insert time with no metric and no log line — previously oversized segments emitted the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and an error log, giving operators visibility; (2) the SpansBuffer `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) no longer has any effect, so operators tuning it will see no change, and it disagrees with the hardcoded 1000 in the Lua script. At minimum, the eviction should emit a metric (e.g. spans evicted per segment) and the hardcoded 1000 should be tied to the configurable max_segment_spans.

findings.title: zpopmin eviction can drop the root/segment span while the has-root-span flag stays set
findings.body: Eviction removes the members with the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores. If the root/segment span of a segment has the oldest end timestamp (common when a parent starts before its children), zpopmin will delete it, yet the script still sets the span-buf:hrs:* key to "1" and the segment continues to be flushed on the short root timeout. The flushed segment then contains no span whose span_id equals the segment id, so `is_segment` is false for every span in the output and downstream consumers that rely on a segment span get a headerless segment. There is no guard preventing eviction of the span that defines the set key.

findings.title: Redirect-following loop cap silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with the explanatory comment deleted
findings.body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. If a trace's redirect chain in span-buf:sr:* exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits without resolving the final set key, and the script writes the span and the new redirect into an intermediate key, permanently splitting the segment (spans land in two different segment sets that flush separately). This is a silent, unexplained 10x reduction of a documented correctness bound; either restore the bound or justify and document the new limit.

findings.title: end_timestamp_precise accessed with [] although the field is optional in the schema
findings.body: process_batch now reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] on every message. In the ingest-spans v1 schema the *_timestamp_precise fields are optional (they were added later for newer SDKs/Relay versions), so messages produced by older producers or replayed from spillover topics that lack the field will raise KeyError inside the processing strategy, which halts the consumer for that partition rather than skipping or defaulting the message. Use val.get("end_timestamp_precise") with a fallback (e.g. the required end_timestamp or 0) so one old message cannot wedge ingestion.

findings.title: No tests for the new eviction behavior or for any of the pagination changes
findings.body: The PR's headline feature — evicting the oldest spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members — has no test anywhere: test_buffer.py only gained end_timestamp_precise fields on existing fixtures. There is no test that a >1000-span segment is truncated to 1000, that eviction prefers the oldest end_timestamp_precise, or that the segment/root span survives. Separately, the large pagination half of this PR (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the negative-offset paths in BasePaginator/Cursor, and the optimized_pagination branch of the audit-logs endpoint) ships with zero tests, and it is entirely unrelated to the PR's stated purpose of span buffer insertion, which makes it impossible to validate intent from the diff.

findings.title: Comments claim negative offsets are a supported performance optimization
findings.body: The only change to Cursor is two comments asserting that negative offsets are an allowed 'performance optimization' enabling 'efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets'. Nothing in Cursor enforces or implements this, and as noted for the paginator changes, Django-backed paginators cannot slice with negative bounds at all. These comments document behavior that does not exist and will mislead future readers into relying on it.
